summary: This Dockerfile creates an Ubuntu container with Zsh shell and Oh-My-Zsh framework pre-installed, then sets up a demo Git repository with nested directories to showcase Zsh's productivity features. When you run the container, you get an interactive login shell that starts deep inside a Git repo, with a custom prompt showing a whale emoji to remind you you're in a container.

explanations.3: This tells Docker to skip interactive prompts during package installation—otherwise the build would hang waiting for user input that never comes.
explanations.5: The `&&` chains commands together and stops if any fail, which is important here because we want to ensure apt-get succeeds before trying to install packages.
explanations.11: After installing packages, we delete the cached package lists to shrink the final image size since we won't need them again.
explanations.15: This downloads and runs the Oh-My-Zsh installer script from the internet, piping it directly to a shell interpreter (a common pattern for one-liners).
explanations.16: The empty string `""` replaces the normal first argument to the installer script, and the flags tell it to run without asking questions and keep the default config file.
explanations.21: These lines configure Git with a dummy user so the demo repository can make commits—Git requires this metadata before it'll let you commit anything.
explanations.31: This sets the container's default working directory, so when you connect to the shell, you land deep in the folder tree where Oh-My-Zsh's shortcuts are most useful.
explanations.37: The `-i` flag makes the shell interactive (reads your commands), and `-l` makes it a login shell (loads your `.zshrc` config file with the custom prompt).
